name: Japan
description: Island empire of unbroken imperial lineage, legendary samurai military codes, Buddhist Zen sanctuaries, wooden architectural masterpieces, and distinct feudal shogunate eras.

sections.heading: Key Developments
content: First permanent imperial capital at Nara

kingdoms.title: Asuka & Nara Periods
kingdoms.description: Formative imperial era characterized by the introduction of Buddhism, Chinese legal systems (Ritsuryo), and the construction of the colossal Great Buddha at Todai-ji.

kingdoms.title: Edo (Tokugawa) Shogunate
kingdoms.description: Establishment of Tokugawa rule following Battle of Sekigahara

sections.heading: Pax Tokugawa
content: Establishment of Tokugawa rule following Battle of Sekigahara
Growth of Edo into one of the world's largest metropolises
Flourishing of Kabuki, Ukiyo-e woodblock art, and Haiku

kingdoms.title: Heian Period
kingdoms.description: Peak of imperial court refinement in Kyoto

sections.heading: Cultural Zenith
content: Peak of imperial court refinement in Kyoto
Dominance of the Fujiwara clan regents
Rise of Minamoto and Taira military clans

kingdoms.title: Heian Period (Classical Imperial Court)
kingdoms.description: The classical zenith of Japanese imperial court culture, poetry, aesthetics, and literature, producing Murasaki Shikibu's Tale of Genji.

kingdoms.title: Kamakura Shogunate
kingdoms.description: The birth of Japanese samurai rule under Minamoto no Yoritomo, introducing the feudal shogunate system and repelling the Mongol invasions.

kingdoms.title: Muromachi & Sengoku Jidai
kingdoms.description: Ashikaga Shogunate and Kitayama culture (Golden Pavilion)

sections.heading: War & Unification
content: Ashikaga Shogunate and Kitayama culture (Golden Pavilion)
Onin War triggering nationwide warlord warfare (Sengoku Jidai)
Unification campaigns of Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi

kingdoms.title: Tokugawa Shogunate (Edo Period)
kingdoms.description: Over 250 years of unbroken internal peace (Pax Tokugawa), rigid social order, urban merchant culture (Ukiyo-e, Kabuki), and strict maritime isolation (Sakoku).

kings.title: Minamoto no Yoritomo (First Shogun)
kings.biography: Founder of the Kamakura Shogunate who defeated the Taira clan in the Genpei War, establishing samurai military government (Bakufu) that endured for nearly seven centuries.
kings.internationalConnections: Consolidated Japanese feudal military institutions while maintaining Buddhist monastic connections with Song China.

kings.title: Oda Nobunaga (The Great Unifier)
kings.biography: First of the Three Great Unifiers of Japan who shattered Sengoku daimyo opposition using massed volley fire matchlock firearms at the Battle of Nagashino and commissioned Azuchi Castle.
kings.internationalConnections: Welcomed Portuguese Jesuit missionaries and patronized European firearms, clockwork, and global cartography.

kings.title: Prince Shotoku (Shotoku Taishi)
kings.biography: Semi-legendary regent who authored Japan's Seventeen-Article Constitution, established the Twelve Level Cap and Rank System, and built Horyu-ji, the world's oldest surviving wooden building.
kings.internationalConnections: Sent formal diplomatic missions to Sui Dynasty China with the famous letter: 'From the Son of Heaven in the land where the sun rises to the Son of Heaven in the land where the sun sets.'

kings.title: Tokugawa Ieyasu
kings.biography: Founder of the Tokugawa Shogunate who unified Japan after victory at the Battle of Sekigahara (1600), creating the prosperous Edo Period that gave rise to samurai culture, Bushido, and urban arts.
kings.internationalConnections: Appointed English navigator William Adams as a samurai advisor and traded with Dutch and English merchant ships.

kings.title: Toyotomi Hideyoshi
kings.biography: Second Great Unifier who rose from peasant foot soldier to Imperial Regent (Kampaku), enforcing nationwide sword hunts, land surveys, and building Osaka Castle.

sites.name: Himeji Castle (White Heron Castle)
sites.description: Japan's most spectacular and best-preserved feudal samurai castle, renowned for its brilliant white plastered wooden walls.
sites.history: Masterpiece of defensive castle architecture that survived the Meiji restoration, World War II bombings, and major earthquakes without damage.
sites.construction: Built on a hill with high curving stone walls (Musha-gaeshi), 83 rooms, and intricate spiral maze defenses.
sites.architecture: Six-story wooden keep with fireproof white plaster, projecting gables, and gun-slit arrow loops.
sites.significance: UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1993; Japan's premier national treasure.
sites.currentStatus: Standing pristine in Himeji, Hyogo Prefecture, Japan.

sites.name: Kinkaku-ji (Golden Pavilion)
sites.description: Iconic Zen Buddhist temple in Kyoto covered in pure gold leaf, reflecting seamlessly across the Kyoko-chi mirror pond.

sites.name: Todai-ji Temple (Eastern Great Temple)
sites.description: Monumental Buddhist temple housing the Daibutsu (15-meter bronze Great Buddha), one of the world's largest wooden buildings.
sites.history: Constructed by Emperor Shomu to bring national unity, peace, and spiritual protection to Japan after epidemics and rebellions.
sites.construction: Built from massive ancient cedar pillars and bronze casting using an estimated 500 tonnes of copper, tin, and gold leaf.
sites.architecture: Massive hip-and-gable roof structure with double eaves and dramatic golden Shibi roof ridge ornaments.
sites.significance: UNESCO World Heritage Site as part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara.
sites.currentStatus: Active temple and national treasure in Nara, Japan.
